Copper is a vital nutrient across a broad variety of taxa and biomolecules [@wrightBacterialEvolutionaryPrecursors2021; @tangMolecularEvolutionCu2025; @lutsenkoMammalianCopperHomeostasis2025], a mainstay of electronics manufacturing, a potent biocide [@weberMarineBiofoulingRole2023], and a key environmental pollutant. Since the 1900s, global copper mining has grown by more than 900% [@pietrzykTrendsGlobalCopper2018a], and demand is predicted to grow substantially further by 2100 [@schipperEstimatingGlobalCopper2018]. Multiple projects aim to exploit Arctic resources to meet this demand, most notably the planned reopening of the Nussir/Ulveryggen copper deposits in Finnmark, northern Norway [@eilertsenNussirGetsOperating2019]. Concurrently, aquaculture, historically an important source of copper emissions (primarily from antifouling net coatings, but also fish feed) to the marine environment, is predicted to grow substantially [@dnvOceansFuture20502021]. Brake wear, soil loss, and copper-based pesticide applications, all important sources of copper emissions to water [@comberSourcesCopperEuropean2023], may also grow as populations and resource exploitation grow in the Arctic, and changing climates enable new forms of agriculture.

The Arctic landscape itself is predicted to undergo significant climatic and ecological changes in the coming century. Receding sea ice will open new shipping routes [@smithNewTransArcticShipping2013]. Warmer temperatures may make resource extraction more economical, although reduced permafrost may also impact infrastructure [@krogerSocioecologicalCrisesGlobal2023]. All ecosystems are highly likely to undergo shifts in species, structure, and phenology, while human populations and economies may be vulnerable to extreme and unpredictable weather [@ipccClimateChange20222023].

## Aggregate Exposure Pathways

The Aggregate Exposure Pathway (AEP) [@teeguardenCompletingLinkExposure2016; @tanAggregateExposurePathways2018] concept was developed in 2016 as an exposure-based counterpart to the Adverse Outcome Pathway (AOP). AOPs assemble evidence to causally link stressor exposure to biological effects in organisms. AEPs do the same for the emission, transport and fate of stressors in the environment, up until the point they reach sensitive tissues or organs in selected organisms.

An AEP is a framework for capturing and structuring knowledge organised as a directed graph (@fig-copper-exposure-aep): Nodes are Key Exposure States (KESs), which represent the qualitative or quantitative state of a stressor(s) in space and time. KES are linked by Key Transitional Relationships (KTR), the transport or transformation of said stressor(s). An AEP has two specialised types of KES, a stressor Source and a Target Site Exposure (TSE), representing the state of a stressor at its origin and site of action respectively [@tanAggregateExposurePathways2018]. The TSE corresponds to the initiating Key Event of an AOP (the Molecular Initiating Event). Thus, an AEP and AOP that cover the same stressor are integrated to create a full Source-to-Outcome Pathway. AOPs have seen rapid uptake in the ecotoxicological community: at the time of writing, 591 AOPs have been drafted or published [@societyforadvancementofaopsAOPwikiV272026]. Conversely, AEPs have seen less adoption (26 hits for "aggregate exposure pathway" in Web of Science's Core Collection [@clarivateCitationReportAggregate2026]).

<!-- Could talk about representing AEPs with different levels of biological organisation here, but it's probably unneeded. -->

A Weight of Evidence (WoE) approach is key to the construction of both AEPs and AOPs [@teeguardenCompletingLinkExposure2016; @tanAggregateExposurePathways2018; @tanRefiningAggregateExposure2018]. Although both represent highly complex, interconnected systems, these networks can be deconstructed into a set of testable linear relationships whose causality can be evaluated using WoE approaches. Consensus and formal standards have emerged in the AOP community on how WoE should be assessed, and @beckerIncreasingScientificConfidence2015 has proposed the use of a modified form of the Bradford-Hill epidemiological criteria [@hillEnvironmentDiseaseAssociation1965] to assess the biological plausibility, empirical support, and essentiality of an AOP's Key Events (KEs). WoE approaches for AEPs are less mature. @pengAggregateExposurePathways2022, which represents the most sophisticated and relevant (that is, it focuses on pollution of the environment and wildlife) AEP of which we are aware, adapts OECD guidance on AOP development [@oecdUsersHandbookSupplement2018] as a basis for developing principles of WoE assessment applicable to AEPs.

## Copper Exposure and Effects

Copper is perhaps ecotoxicology's most studied single pollutant [@grandjeanMatthewEffectEnvironmental2011]. Analytical techniques are mature, and the metal is routinely monitored in the environment. However, as a lower-priority pollutant it has received less attention in Arctic monitoring. For example, the Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Programme, which synthesises Arctic pollutant monitoring , last reported on copper in 2002 [@arcticmonitoringandassessmentprogrammeAMAPAssessment20022005].

Copper is naturally present in the earth's crust and seawater, and enters marine environments from a variety of sources. At a European level, the primary anthropogenic sources of copper to the aquatic environment are vehicle brake wear, animal manure, and antifoulants on commercial shipping, while soil loss is the most substantial natural source [@comberSourcesCopperEuropean2023]. At individual sites, sources such as mining, aquaculture, and leisure craft antifoulants may also be important sources, as well as historical contamination from industrial activities [@helcomCopperHELCOMCore2023; @sternalImpactSubmarineCopper2017; @grosvikKunnskapsstotteOmMiljoeffekter2023]. In general, copper's occurrence and bioavailability are highly spatially specific, and the highest concentrations of dissolved copper (generally the most bioavailable and toxic fraction [@anzgToxicantDefaultGuideline2026]) are found in areas with substantial local emissions and limited water turnover (e.g. marinas, inner fjords) [@steinnesEvidenceLargeScale1997; @grosvikKunnskapsstotteOmMiljoeffekter2023; @sternalImpactSubmarineCopper2017; @lagerstromFlawedRiskAssessment2020].

Copper's toxicity to marine organisms is remarkably complex, depending both on its presence in bioavailable forms, and environmental factors such as local pH, temperature, and the presence of both complexing agents (i.e. dissolved organic carbon) and competing binding ions [@raderFateCopperAdded2019; @mebaneBioavailabilityToxicityModels2023; @nysDerivationBioavailabilitybasedEnvironmental2026]. Copper uptake and exposure (@fig-copper-exposure-aep) in fish and aquatic invertebrates is primarily through gills (waterborne, dissolved copper), but also via the digestive system (dietary copper) and integument [@carvalhoEffectCopperLiver2008; @casado-martinezAssessingMetalBioaccumulation2013; @ahearnMechanismsHeavymetalSequestration2004], the relative magnitude of these exposure routes depending on the habitat, feeding strategy, and life stage of an organism, as well as local conditions.

The importance of different routes and sites will depend on species diet, lifestyle, life stage, and anatomy; for example, not all marine invertebrates have gills or a hepatopancreas. Not all Target Sites of Exposure/linkages to toxicity modes of action are included. Dashed lines represent KES whose relevance depends on specific organismal biology.](figures/fig01-example-aep.png){#fig-copper-exposure-aep}

In fish and aquatic invertebrates, acute toxicity is driven by disruption of ionoregulation (largely of sodium) [@mebaneBioavailabilityToxicityModels2023a; @anzgToxicantDefaultGuideline2026; @vernonAssessingRelativeSensitivity2019], which principally occurs in epithelial cells in the gill and gut [@maNovelCopperResponsiveCell2025]. Damage to sensory organs - which induces maladaptive behaviour - by sub-chronic copper concentrations is also attested in the literature for fish [@mebaneBioavailabilityToxicityModels2023a; @liaoToxicityMechanismsBioavailability2023] and aquatic invertebrates [@pyleCopperimpairedChemosensoryFunction2007; @lahmanSublethalCopperToxicity2015]. Beyond ionoregulation, copper toxicity is also mediated by generation of Reactive Oxygen Species, alterations to the electron-transfer chain within mitochondria, endocrine disruption, and (in fish, not depicted in @fig-copper-exposure-aep) disruption to ammonia excretion and acid-base balance [@liaoToxicityMechanismsBioavailability2023]. Chronic exposure to copper is also suspected to result in an elevated "energy cost", which may impair survival, lifespans, and reproduction of affected populations [@mebaneBioavailabilityToxicityModels2023a].

All organisms have mechanisms for maintaining copper homeostasis: in fish, excess copper is typically stored in the liver, where it is both used as an essential nutrient and excreted to bile, [@mebaneBioavailabilityToxicityModels2023a] and muscle tissue. In many invertebrates, the hepatopancreas both absorbs copper from the diet and sequesters excess copper [@ahearnMechanismsHeavymetalSequestration2004]; excess copper may also be stored in hard tissues [@martinsCopperUptakeBlue2026]. In many molluscs and crustaceans, copper plays an additional role as a component of haemocyanin, an oxygen-transport metalloprotein analogous to haemoglobin [@banaeeAssessingMetalToxicity2024].

<!-- @mebaneBioavailabilityToxicityModels2023a notes that diet is the principle source of bioaccumulated copper in freshwater aquatic invertebrates (in low-Cu environments), but that it is unclear whether dietary copper is an important mediator of adverse effects in most species/ecosystems. @campanaSubLethalEffectsCopper2012 study of sediment-based exposure to marine benthic organisms' found that dietary exposure's importance as a route depends substantially on the sediment composition and feeding strategy of individual species.  -->

In algae, copper ions that bind (passively) to the cell wall are actively transported by one or more systems across the cell membrane [@kongCopperRequirementAcquisition2022a], to maintain optimal intracellular balance. Responses to excess ambient copper may include downregulation of copper uptake systems, the synthesis of extracellular ligands to reduce Cu binding to the cell [@kongCopperRequirementAcquisition2022a], liganding, and sequestration. Both algal sensitivity to copper and relevant modes of action vary considerably between species groups [@stauberUseLimitationsMicrobial2011]. Copper toxicity to algae is believed to occur externally via effects to the cell membrane [@anzgToxicantDefaultGuideline2026] and internally via disruption of photosynthesis, cellular pH, or enzyme formation [@stauberUseLimitationsMicrobial2011; @connanImpactsAmbientSalinity2011].

<!-- Note from a closer reading of @wangHomeostaticRegulationCopper2016 - they suggest that the liver is the main hub for copper storage and redistribution, but also that the carcass - mostly muscle tissue, >50% of body mass - is probably a large sink for copper and thus also plays an important role. -->

Modelling and predicting copper's emissions to, behaviour in, and toxicity to species inhabiting marine environments remains challenging [@pedersenImpactsClimateChange2022; @helcomCopperHELCOMCore2023; @comberFutureCopperLoads2025]. It is suggested that increases in marine temperatures and acidity will drive an increase in both leaching from marine occurrences (both natural and anthropogenic) [@pedersenImpactsClimateChange2022] and species sensitivity [@cuiComprehensiveAssessmentCoppers2024]. Should the demand for and use of copper increase concurrently with species' sensitivity to copper, its importance as a stressor may grow substantially.

In this paper, we propose a conceptual AEP and use it as a framework to identify the KESs and guide the capture and organisation of relevant exposure data for marine fish, invertebrates, and algae. We identify and review available Arctic copper exposure and emissions data from scientific literature, environmental monitoring campaigns, and a national pollutant registry. From these data, quantitative, spatially explicit AEPs are constructed to describe and evaluate how copper from multiple natural and anthropogenic sources is transported to and within two marine case studies in the Arctic. We assess the WoE for emissions, occurrence, and exposure of organisms, and evaluate available exposure evidence against our conceptual AEP. Finally, the state of current knowledge on copper exposure in case study Arctic ecosystems is characterised, and knowledge gaps identified.
